glosses: An item of information put into a temporary or permanent physical medium.

examples.text: The person had a record of the interview so she could review her notes.
The tourist's photographs and the tape of the police call provide a record of the crime.
He draws eclectically on studies of baboons, descriptive anthropological accounts of hunter-gatherer societies and, in a few cases, the fossil record.

glosses: Any instance of a physical medium on which information was put for the purpose of preserving it and making it available for future reference.

examples.text: We have no record of you making this payment to us.

glosses: Ellipsis of phonograph record (“a disc, usually made from vinyl, on which sound is recorded and may be replayed on a phonograph”).

examples.text: I still like records better than CDs.
He's the record doctor / Tell him your woes / He'll reach in his bag / And he'll give you a dose

glosses: A set of data relating to a single individual or item.

examples.text: Pull up the record on John Smith. What's his medical history?

glosses: A data structure similar to a struct, in some programming languages such as C and Java based on classes and designed for storing immutable data.

examples.text: This chapter examines another data structure, the record (available in Pascal but not in all other high-level languages). Records make it easier to organize and represent information in Pascal, a major reason for the popularity of the Pascal[…]
The new record type provides another solution. A record is a class-like construct for data classes, a restricted form of class like enums and annotations.
A record is a special kind of class that's designed to work well with immutable (readonly) data.

glosses: The most extreme known value of some variable, particularly that of an achievement in competitive events.

examples.text: The heat and humidity were both new records.
Australia set a record of 10 back-to-back T20I wins.
He broke the record for the youngest English captain.
The team set a new record for most points scored in a game.

"Avanti has literally broken records over the last six months for delays and cancellations, and the Conservatives' answer is to reward failure with millions more in taxpayer cash," said Labour Shadow Transport Secretary Louise Haigh.

glosses: Enough to break previous records and set a new one; world-class; historic.

examples.text: "But it's far worse for me," said Edmund, "because you'll at least have a room of your own and I shall have to share a bedroom with that record stinker, Eustace."

glosses: To make a record of information.

examples.text: I wanted to record every detail of what happened, for the benefit of future generations.

The display and result must be placed in the context that was it was against a side that looked every bit their Fifa world ranking of 141 - but England completed the job with efficiency to record their biggest away win in 19 years.

glosses: To make an audio or video recording of.

examples.text: Within a week they had recorded both the song and the video for it.

glosses: To give legal status to by making an official public record.

examples.text: When the deed was recorded, we officially owned the house.

glosses: To fix in a medium, usually in a tangible medium.
To make an audio, video, or multimedia recording.
To repeat; to practice.
To sing or repeat a tune.

examples.text: Une saisie réelle est nulle, si elle n’est enregistrée.

glosses: Constater, noter, remarquer.

examples.text: Lors d’un point presse jeudi, Météo-France a reconnu avoir été « surprise par les valeurs des rafales », « tout à fait exceptionnelles ». Les plus fortes ont été enregistrées à Marignana (225 km/h), à L’Île-Rousse (206 km/h) et à Calvi (197 km/h)
